newsitem.title: FRANCE: Kinnock aims to slash road deaths by a third.
newsitem.headline: Kinnock aims to slash road deaths by a third.

text.p: The annual toll of 45,000 people killed on European Union roads could be slashed by more than a third come 2010 by technical advances and tighter laws, the European Commission said on Wednesday.
"The human cost of this carnage which shatters lives and plunges entire families into misery is obvious and beyond measure," EU Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock told a news conference.

"And it is accompanied by a very heavy financial cost - arising from medical care, emergency services and lost output - which is estimated at 45 billion ecus ($51 billion) a year, one million for every person killed," he said.
Kinnock said the number of victims, which in 1995 included 1.6 million people injured, could drop 15 percentage points if people equalled the seat-belt wearing record of the best country.

Further cuts could come from better design of car safety features to lessen pedestrian injuries, the fitting of vehicle collision warning systems or "smart" speed governors, road layout changes and the fitting of day-running lights on all vehicles.
Obligatory measures for repeat drink-drivers exceeding allowed blood-alcohol limits would help cut the number of deaths in drink-related crashes.

"The Commission believes that adoption of this strategy would lead to a progressive reduction in the number of annual road fatalities of up to at least 18,000 persons by the year 2010," the draft text said.

European Commission figures put Portugal top of the EU table of people killed per million cars registered, with 1,043 killed in 1994. Next came Greece, with 987 people killed, Spain, Ireland and Austria, with 453, 449 and 385 deaths respectively.
At the other end of the scale came Sweden's 164, followed by Britain and the Netherlands, who recorded 168 and 221 deaths respectively.

Kinnock's remarks came as the European Parliament nodded through rules to harmonise the conditions under which motorists are authorised to drive in the EU, including minimum age and vision requirements, motoring skills and vehicle categories.

The parliament reluctantly accepted there was insufficient support among EU governments for their demand that dangerous drivers who lose their licence in one EU member state should be banned from driving throughout the Union, something Kinnock said he also regretted.
National officials have been discussing mutual recognition of driving penalties for over eight years but legal and practical difficulties have blocked an agreement. ($=0.88 ecu)
